items.stem: Which term matches this description: "The specialist vocabulary listed in or implied by the case study that students must be able to define and apply"?
options: pre-released case study
challenge question
computational solution
technical terminology (case study)
items.answer: technical terminology (case study)
items.markingKey: D. This is the definition of technical terminology (case study).

items.stem: "The case study only requires knowledge of the technologies named in it." Explain the flaw in this statement.
items.answer: Questions may test related concepts, alternatives and their implications; research should cover the wider computer science the scenario relies on.
items.markingKey: Questions may test related concepts, alternatives and their implications; research should cover the wider computer science the scenario relies on. 1 mark for identifying the error, 1-2 marks for the correct explanation.

items.stem: Explain the difference between a stakeholder and a user.
items.answer: A user directly interacts with the system; a stakeholder is anyone affected by or interested in it, including users, managers, developers, regulators and the public.
items.markingKey: A user directly interacts with the system; a stakeholder is anyone affected by or interested in it, including users, managers, developers, regulators and the public. One mark for a correct account of each side; further marks for making the difference explicit (not two separate definitions).

items.stem: Lakeside International School in Geneva keeps student, course and grade data in a relational database, uses an ML model to flag students who may need support, and writes its timetabling tool in Python. Outline the interests of two stakeholder groups, such as drivers and teachers, in the proposed system, and identify one way in which their interests might conflict.
items.answer: drivers: fair pay and allocation, transparency of algorithms; teachers: accurate data, workload, student privacy. Conflict: e.g. efficiency/cost goals vs privacy, fairness or transparency for individuals.
items.markingKey: drivers: fair pay and allocation, transparency of algorithms; teachers: accurate data, workload, student privacy 1 mark per stakeholder interest (with context), 1-2 marks for a plausible conflict.

items.stem: NordLib, a group of public libraries in Oslo, runs a loans database, recommends books with a clustering model and maintains a catalogue application written in Java. One challenge identified in the case study is predicting demand when historical data is sparse or biased. Identify the area of computer science this challenge relates to and outline two possible approaches.
items.answer: Area: data quality and ML bias. Approaches: data augmentation, collecting more representative data, transfer learning, monitoring for drift, human oversight.
items.markingKey: Area/concept identified: data quality and ML bias (1). Approaches/concepts: data augmentation, collecting more representative data, transfer learning, monitoring for drift, human oversight – 1 mark per relevant, context-specific point (max 3).

items.stem:
Case study context: Alpine Rescue in Vienna logs mountain incidents with GPS coordinates in a spatial database, predicts avalanche risk from weather features and coordinates teams with an OOP dispatch system.
(a) Explain why students should research beyond the text of the case study. Refer to Alpine Rescue in Vienna in your answer. [3]
(b) Analyse one strength and one limitation of the view that Studying a pre-released case study gives an unfair advantage to students with more time for research. Refer to Alpine Rescue in Vienna in your answer. [3]
items.answer: (a) Examination questions can ask about the underlying technologies, alternatives and ethical issues in more depth than the case study explains; additional research gives the technical knowledge needed to analyse and evaluate. (b) The case study is designed to be accessible; fairness depends mostly on structured school preparation rather than extra private research.
items.markingKey: (a) [3 marks] Award marks for: Examination questions can ask about the underlying technologies, alternatives and ethical issues in more depth than the case study explains; additional research gives the technical knowledge needed to analyse and evaluate. (one for each linked point in the chain of reasoning; no marks for assertion without explanation.) (b) [3 marks] Arguments for: access to resources and time varies; some topics may be unfamiliar to some cultures. Arguments against: all students receive it months in advance; questions reward understanding over volume of research; schools guide preparation. Supported judgement: The case study is designed to be accessible; fairness depends mostly on structured school preparation rather than extra private research. Credit is given only for points applied to the stated organisation (not generic answers).

items.stem: Which of the following best describes "technical terminology (case study)"?
options: Collecting the client's needs through interviews, questionnaires, observation or analysing existing systems
A table used to record the values of variables step by step as an algorithm runs, to check its logic
The specialist vocabulary listed in or implied by the case study that students must be able to define and apply
The longest sequence of dependent tasks in a project, which determines the minimum completion time
items.answer: The specialist vocabulary listed in or implied by the case study that students must be able to define and apply
items.markingKey: C. "technical terminology (case study)" is the specialist vocabulary listed in or implied by the case study that students must be able to define and apply.

items.stem: Explain why it is useful to build a glossary while studying the case study.
items.answer: Questions often require precise definitions; a glossary of the technical terms with examples from the scenario helps answer "define" and "explain" questions accurately and consistently.

items.stem: In IB Computer Science examinations, which description matches the command term "Construct"?
options: Give an account of similarities and differences between two (or more) items or situations, referring to both throughout.
Display information in a diagrammatic or logical form.
Provide an answer from a number of possibilities.
Give a specific name, value or other brief answer without explanation or calculation.
items.answer: Display information in a diagrammatic or logical form.
items.markingKey: B. Construct: Display information in a diagrammatic or logical form.

items.stem:
Assertion (A): "State" questions require a detailed explanation.
Reason (R): "State" asks for a specific name, value or brief answer.
Which option is correct?
options: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
A is true but R is false.
A is false but R is true.
items.answer: A is false but R is true.
items.markingKey: D. A is false; R is true.

items.stem: Explain why generic answers score poorly on case-study questions.
items.answer: Markbands reward application to the scenario; a generic list of advantages shows knowledge but not analysis of how it applies to the organisation's specific situation.
items.markingKey: Award marks for: Markbands reward application to the scenario; a generic list of advantages shows knowledge but not analysis of how it applies to the organisation's specific situation. items.stem: Mohammed writes: "Using more technical terms always gains more marks." Explain why this is inaccurate.
items.answer: Terms gain credit only when used accurately and applied to the question; misused jargon earns nothing.
items.markingKey: Terms gain credit only when used accurately and applied to the question; misused jargon earns nothing. 1 mark for identifying the error, 1-2 marks for the correct explanation.

items.stem: Aurora Energy, a utility in Toronto, collects smart-meter readings in a distributed database, detects faults with anomaly detection and models its devices as objects in a simulation. A Paper 1 case-study question reads: "To what extent will the proposed system succeed in reducing the energy use of training and running models?" [8] Describe how a student should structure a high-scoring answer, explaining what the command term requires.
items.answer: To what extent: set out arguments for and against with technical evidence, consider conditions/limitations, and conclude with a clear judgement of extent. Relevant content: smaller or distilled models, efficient hardware, scheduling training when renewable energy is available, choosing low-carbon data centres.
items.markingKey: Command-term requirement: set out arguments for and against with technical evidence, consider conditions/limitations, and conclude with a clear judgement of extent (2). Planned content relevant to environmental impact: smaller or distilled models, efficient hardware, scheduling training when renewable energy is available, choosing low-carbon data centres (1-2). Allocation of time/points to the 8 marks and use of the scenario (1).

items.stem: Give one argument for and one argument against the view that Planning an answer before writing wastes time in a timed examination.
items.answer: A short plan is worthwhile for extended-response questions and saves time overall; it is unnecessary for 1–2 mark items.
items.markingKey: Arguments for: time is limited; some short questions need no plan. Arguments against: for 6–8 mark questions a brief plan ensures balance and a conclusion; reduces repetition and irrelevance; helps meet the command term. Supported judgement: A short plan is worthwhile for extended-response questions and saves time overall; it is unnecessary for 1–2 mark items.

items.stem: Which of the following best describes "mark allocation"?
options: A level descriptor used to mark extended responses holistically, describing the quality of answer needed for each range of marks
The number of marks shown for a question part, indicating how many distinct, developed points are expected
An early working model of the product used to test ideas and gather client feedback
A case-study question in Paper 1 that asks candidates to analyse or evaluate a challenge faced by the organisation using their research
items.answer: The number of marks shown for a question part, indicating how many distinct, developed points are expected
items.markingKey: B. "mark allocation" is the number of marks shown for a question part, indicating how many distinct, developed points are expected.

items.stem: Zara writes: "A six-mark "discuss" question can be answered with a bullet list of six advantages." Explain why this is inaccurate.

items.stem: Which of the following best describes "internal assessment (IA)"?
options: A product, such as an application or system, built through programming to solve the identified problem
The computational solution coursework in which a student develops a product to solve a problem, documents the process and demonstrates the product; it is internally marked and externally moderated
Specific, measurable statements of what the product must do, used to test and evaluate whether it solves the problem
A person or group affected by, or with an interest in, a computer system
items.answer: The computational solution coursework in which a student develops a product to solve a problem, documents the process and demonstrates the product; it is internally marked and externally moderated
items.markingKey: B. "internal assessment (IA)" is the computational solution coursework in which a student develops a product to solve a problem, documents the process and demonstrates the product; it is internally marked and externally moderated.

items.stem: Explain why consultation with a client is important at the start of an IA.
items.answer: It provides evidence of a genuine problem and real requirements, ensures the success criteria reflect what the client needs, and gives a basis for later feedback and evaluation.
items.markingKey: Award marks for: It provides evidence of a genuine problem and real requirements, ensures the success criteria reflect what the client needs, and gives a basis for later feedback and evaluation. (2 marks: one for each linked point in the chain of reasoning; no marks for assertion without explanation.)

items.stem: Explain the difference between test plan and success criteria.
items.answer: Success criteria state what the product must achieve; the test plan describes how each criterion (and each feature) will be tested, with data and expected results.
items.markingKey: Success criteria state what the product must achieve; the test plan describes how each criterion (and each feature) will be tested, with data and expected results. One mark for a correct account of each side; further marks for making the difference explicit (not two separate definitions).

items.stem:
A student's IA proposes the following success criteria. For each one, state whether it is a suitable (specific and testable) success criterion and justify, rewriting any unsuitable criterion.
1. The system allows the club secretary to add, edit and delete member records.
2. The client will be happy with the product.
3. An email reminder is sent to members 24 hours before each event.
items.answer: 1: suitable – specific, testable function; 2: unsuitable – not a measurable feature of the product; 3: suitable – specific and testable
items.markingKey: 1: suitable – specific, testable function; 2: unsuitable – not a measurable feature of the product; 3: suitable – specific and testable 1 mark per correct judgement with justification/rewrite.

items.stem: Lars writes: "A problem specification can be written after the product is finished." Explain why this is inaccurate.
items.answer: It should be developed first, from consultation, because it drives the design and testing.
items.markingKey: It should be developed first, from consultation, because it drives the design and testing. 1 mark for identifying the error, 1-2 marks for the correct explanation.

items.stem:
(a) Define the term "client". [2]
(b) A student's IA proposes the following success criteria. For each one, state whether it is a suitable (specific and testable) success criterion and justify, rewriting any unsuitable criterion.
1. An email reminder is sent to members 24 hours before each event.
2. Passwords are stored as salted hashes, never in plain text.
3. A search by surname returns matching records in under 2 seconds for 5000 records.
4. The app looks nice. [4]
(c) An IA student is developing a computational solution for a youth football league in Bogotá, which needs to store fixtures, results and league tables. Write a problem specification outline: identify the client and problem, justify a computational solution, and propose three specific, testable success criteria. [5]
items.answer: (a) The person or organisation for whom the IA product is developed, whose needs define the problem (b) 1: suitable – specific and testable; 2: suitable – testable by inspecting the database; 3: suitable – measurable performance criterion; 4: unsuitable – subjective and untestable (c) Client/problem: a youth football league in Bogotá currently handles the need to store fixtures, results and league tables manually (paper/spreadsheets), causing errors, lost data and wasted time. Justification: a database-backed application automates storage, validation, searching and reporting. Example criteria: 1) the user can add/edit/delete records with validation of each field; 2) a search returns matching records in under 2 s; 3) the system produces a specified report (e.g. overdue items) on demand.
items.markingKey: (a) [2 marks] 1 mark for the core idea: the person or organisation for whom the IA product is developed, whose needs define the problem. Award full marks only if the defining feature is clear; a vague example alone scores 0. (b) [4 marks] 1: suitable – specific and testable; 2: suitable – testable by inspecting the database; 3: suitable – measurable performance criterion; 4: unsuitable – subjective and untestable 1 mark per correct judgement with justification/rewrite. (c) [5 marks] Client and problem clearly identified with evidence of consultation (1); computational solution justified (1); three specific, measurable, testable success criteria linked to the problem (1 each).

items.stem:
Internal assessment context: A student is developing an IA computational solution for a badminton club in Kuala Lumpur, which needs to track court bookings and member fees.
(a) With the help of a specific example, explain why success criteria must be specific and measurable. Refer to this IA project in your answer. [3]
(b) Outline two points that could be used to evaluate the claim: "A real client is essential for a successful IA." Refer to this IA project in your answer. [3]
items.answer: (a) They are used to test the product and to evaluate it; vague criteria ("easy to use") cannot be shown to be met or not met, while measurable ones ("books a slot in under 30 seconds") can be tested objectively. (A specific, correct example that illustrates this is required for full marks.) (b) A real client strengthens the problem definition and evaluation, though what matters most is a clearly specified, genuine problem with testable criteria.

items.stem:
(a) Explain the difference between a functional requirement and a non-functional requirement. [2]
(b) A student claims that Success criteria should describe the programming techniques used. Identify the error in this claim and correct it. [3]
(c) "A real client is essential for a successful IA." To what extent do you agree with this statement? [8]
items.answer: (a) A functional requirement states what the system must do (add a booking); a non-functional requirement states how well it must do it (response time, security, usability). (b) They describe what the product must do for the client; techniques belong in design and development documentation. (c) A real client strengthens the problem definition and evaluation, though what matters most is a clearly specified, genuine problem with testable criteria.

(c) [8 marks] Arguments for: provides authentic requirements and feedback; evaluation is more meaningful. Arguments against: an adviser or the student acting as user may suffice for some problems; clients can be unavailable or change requirements. items.stem: Explain the difference between beta testing and alpha testing.
items.answer: Alpha testing is done by the developer in a controlled environment; beta testing is done by the client or real users in real conditions.
items.markingKey: Alpha testing is done by the developer in a controlled environment; beta testing is done by the client or real users in real conditions. One mark for a correct account of each side; further marks for making the difference explicit (not two separate definitions).

items.stem: Part of an IA test plan must test the validation of the number of guests per booking, which must be an integer from 1 to 12. Construct 4 rows of the test plan giving the test data, the type of test and the expected result.
items.answer: 5 – normal – accepted; 1 – boundary – accepted; 12 – boundary – accepted; 0 – boundary (just outside) – rejected with error message
items.markingKey: 5 – normal – accepted; 1 – boundary – accepted; 12 – boundary – accepted; 0 – boundary (just outside) – rejected with error message 1 mark per two correct rows (data, type, expected outcome); must include normal, both boundaries and erroneous data.

items.stem:
An IA student plans these tasks:
A Consult client: 3 days, after —
B Design database: 3 days, after A
C Design interface: 3 days, after A
D Code back end: 7 days, after B
E Code front end: 9 days, after C
F Test and fix: 4 days, after D, E
G Evaluate with client: 3 days, after F
Determine the minimum number of days to complete the project and the critical path. Explain why identifying the critical path helps planning.
items.answer: Minimum duration 22 days; critical path A → C → E → F → G. Tasks on the critical path cannot slip without delaying the whole project, so they need closest monitoring; others have float.
items.markingKey: Earliest finish times: A 3, B 6, C 6, D 13, E 15, F 19, G 22 (M1 M1). Minimum duration 22 days; critical path A → C → E → F → G. (A1). R1 explanation.

items.stem:

B Design database: 5 days, after A
C Design interface: 3 days, after A
D Code back end: 7 days, after B
E Code front end: 7 days, after C
F Test and fix: 4 days, after D, E

Tasks on the critical path cannot slip without delaying the whole project, so they need closest monitoring; others have float. (c) Tests must also include boundary and erroneous data to show robust validation and error handling.

(c) [3 marks] Tests must also include boundary and erroneous data to show robust validation and error handling. 1 mark for identifying the error, 1-2 marks for the correct explanation.

items.stem:
Internal assessment context: A student is developing an IA computational solution for a family bakery in Lisbon, which needs to record daily orders and stock of ingredients.
(a) Explain the difference between alpha testing and beta testing. Refer to this IA project in your answer. [3]
(b) Give one argument for and one argument against the view that Agile, iterative development is better than a linear (waterfall) approach for an IA. Refer to this IA project in your answer. [3]
items.answer: (a) Alpha testing is done by the developer in a controlled environment; beta testing is done by the client or real users in real conditions. (b) For most IAs an iterative approach with clear documentation works best, provided the overall plan and deadlines are kept under control.
items.markingKey: (a) [3 marks] Alpha testing is done by the developer in a controlled environment; beta testing is done by the client or real users in real conditions. (b) [3 marks] Arguments for: frequent client feedback improves fit to needs; problems found early; flexible when requirements change. Arguments against: harder to plan a fixed timeline; documentation of each iteration takes time; waterfall suits well-defined, stable requirements. Supported judgement: For most IAs an iterative approach with clear documentation works best, provided the overall plan and deadlines are kept under control. Credit is given only for points applied to the stated organisation (not generic answers).

items.stem:
(a) State what is meant by the term "mark allocation". [2]
(b) A student claims that a six-mark "discuss" question can be answered with a bullet list of six advantages. Identify the error in this claim and correct it. [2]
(c) MetroFlow, the public-transport authority in Kuala Lumpur, stores ticketing data in a data warehouse, predicts passenger demand with machine learning and runs route-planning software built from classes and graph structures. A Paper 1 case-study question reads: "To what extent will the proposed system succeed in scaling the system to millions of users at peak times?" [8] Describe how a student should structure a high-scoring answer, explaining what the command term requires. [4]
items.answer: (a) The number of marks shown for a question part, indicating how many distinct, developed points are expected (b) It needs a balanced, developed argument with points on more than one side, applied to the scenario, and a conclusion. (c) To what extent: set out arguments for and against with technical evidence, consider conditions/limitations, and conclude with a clear judgement of extent. Relevant content: horizontal scaling, load balancing, caching, distributed or NoSQL databases, cloud auto-scaling.

items.stem:
(a) Outline the meaning of the term "recommendations for improvement". [2]
(b) Isabel writes: "The video should be as long as possible to show everything." Explain why this is inaccurate. [2]
(c) An IA student recorded these test results against the success criteria:
Criterion: search in under 1 s; evidence: times 1.37, 0.51, 1.27, 1.08, 1.34 s
Criterion: at least 95% of test bookings processed correctly; evidence: 99% correct
Criterion: a booking takes at most 5 clicks; evidence: 3 clicks
State whether each criterion was met, and suggest one improvement for any criterion that was not met. [4]
items.answer: (a) Realistic, specific suggestions for further development based on the evaluation (b) It should be concise and focused on demonstrating that the product works and meets its success criteria. (c) "search in under 1 s": times 1.37, 0.51, 1.27, 1.08, 1.34 s → not met; "at least 95% of test bookings processed correctly": 99% correct → met; "a booking takes at most 5 clicks": 3 clicks → met. Improvements: e.g. add an index/optimise query for speed; fix validation logic for accuracy; simplify the booking form for clicks.
items.markingKey: (a) [2 marks] 1 mark for the core idea: realistic, specific suggestions for further development based on the evaluation. (b) [2 marks] It should be concise and focused on demonstrating that the product works and meets its success criteria. 1 mark for identifying the error, 1-2 marks for the correct explanation. (c) [4 marks] "search in under 1 s": times 1.37, 0.51, 1.27, 1.08, 1.34 s → not met; "at least 95% of test bookings processed correctly": 99% correct → met; "a booking takes at most 5 clicks": 3 clicks → met 1 mark per correct judgement referring to the evidence; 1 mark for a realistic improvement linked to an unmet criterion.

items.stem:
A student's IA proposes the following success criteria. For each one, state whether it is a suitable (specific and testable) success criterion and justify, rewriting any unsuitable criterion.
1. The program works well.
2. The client will be happy with the product.
3. A search by surname returns matching records in under 2 seconds for 5000 records.
4. The teacher can export a class's grades as a CSV file that opens in a spreadsheet.
items.answer: 1: unsuitable – not specific or measurable; 2: unsuitable – not a measurable feature of the product; 3: suitable – measurable performance criterion; 4: suitable – specific and testable
items.markingKey: 1: unsuitable – not specific or measurable; 2: unsuitable – not a measurable feature of the product; 3: suitable – measurable performance criterion; 4: suitable – specific and testable 1 mark per correct judgement with justification/rewrite.

items.stem:
Internal assessment context: A student is developing an IA computational solution for a youth football league in Bogotá, which needs to store fixtures, results and league tables.
(a) Explain the difference between black-box testing and white-box testing. Refer to this IA project in your answer. [3]
(b) Analyse one strength and one limitation of the view that Agile, iterative development is better than a linear (waterfall) approach for an IA. Refer to this IA project in your answer. [3]
items.answer: (a) White-box testing uses knowledge of the code to test paths and branches; black-box testing checks outputs for given inputs against the specification without looking at the code. (b) For most IAs an iterative approach with clear documentation works best, provided the overall plan and deadlines are kept under control.
items.markingKey: (a) [3 marks] White-box testing uses knowledge of the code to test paths and branches; black-box testing checks outputs for given inputs against the specification without looking at the code. One mark for a correct account of each side; further marks for making the difference explicit (not two separate definitions). (b) [3 marks] Arguments for: frequent client feedback improves fit to needs; problems found early; flexible when requirements change. Arguments against: harder to plan a fixed timeline; documentation of each iteration takes time; waterfall suits well-defined, stable requirements. Supported judgement: For most IAs an iterative approach with clear documentation works best, provided the overall plan and deadlines are kept under control. Credit is given only for points applied to the stated organisation (not generic answers).

items.stem:
Case study context: Alpine Rescue in Vienna logs mountain incidents with GPS coordinates in a spatial database, predicts avalanche risk from weather features and coordinates teams with an OOP dispatch system.
(a) Explain why students should research beyond the text of the case study. Refer to Alpine Rescue in Vienna in your answer. [2]
(b) To what extent is it true that Studying a pre-released case study gives an unfair advantage to students with more time for research? Refer to Alpine Rescue in Vienna in your answer. [4]
items.answer: (a) Examination questions can ask about the underlying technologies, alternatives and ethical issues in more depth than the case study explains; additional research gives the technical knowledge needed to analyse and evaluate. (b) The case study is designed to be accessible; fairness depends mostly on structured school preparation rather than extra private research.
items.markingKey: (a) [2 marks] Award marks for: Examination questions can ask about the underlying technologies, alternatives and ethical issues in more depth than the case study explains; additional research gives the technical knowledge needed to analyse and evaluate. (one for each linked point in the chain of reasoning; no marks for assertion without explanation.) (b) [4 marks] Arguments for: access to resources and time varies; some topics may be unfamiliar to some cultures. Arguments against: all students receive it months in advance; questions reward understanding over volume of research; schools guide preparation. Supported judgement: The case study is designed to be accessible; fairness depends mostly on structured school preparation rather than extra private research. items.stem:
Case study context: Lakeside International School in Geneva keeps student, course and grade data in a relational database, uses an ML model to flag students who may need support, and writes its timetabling tool in Python.
(a) A student claims that Using more technical terms always gains more marks. Identify the error in this claim and correct it. Refer to Lakeside International School in Geneva in your answer. [2]
(b) Evaluate the claim that Planning an answer before writing wastes time in a timed examination. Refer to Lakeside International School in Geneva in your answer. [4]
items.answer: (a) Terms gain credit only when used accurately and applied to the question; misused jargon earns nothing. (b) A short plan is worthwhile for extended-response questions and saves time overall; it is unnecessary for 1–2 mark items.

items.stem: "Client feedback is more valuable than test results in an IA evaluation." To what extent do you agree with this statement?
items.answer: The strongest evaluations combine objective test evidence with client feedback for each success criterion.
items.markingKey: Arguments for: shows whether the product meets real needs; reveals usability issues tests may miss. Arguments against: feedback can be subjective or polite; tests provide objective, repeatable evidence; both are needed to judge each criterion. Supported judgement: The strongest evaluations combine objective test evidence with client feedback for each success criterion. Markbands (8 marks): top band: well-balanced discussion with accurate, specific technical detail applied to the context and a justified conclusion; middle band: some balance and correct terminology, conclusion only partly supported; bottom band: descriptive, largely one-sided, little technical detail or application.
